Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-22
Start: 15:30 PT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Thompson (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Sara Alvarez (CTO, Comet), Ravi Patel (Backend Lead), Nina Gomez (Infosec), Omar Ruiz (ML Eng)

Summary (auto): discuss p95 latency targets, concurrency, streaming behavior, token/sec benchmarking, and deployment options (hosted vs dedicated vs private). Customer wants sub-250ms p95 for 256-token responses at 5 concurrent streams, and guidance on throughput and cost tradeoffs.

Topics: p95 targets; concurrency; streaming; prefix / KV cache; quantization; dedicated capacity sizing; security and compliance (SOC2, KMS); benchmarking plan and next steps.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Thompson: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. This is Maya from Redwood, AE on this account. With me is Liam Chen, our solutions engineer.
[00:08] Sara Alvarez: Hey Maya, hi Liam, thanks. We have about an hour. I'm Sara, CTO at Comet Payments. Also Ravi, Nina and Omar here.
[00:15] Liam Chen: Great, quick agenda: understand your latency p95 and concurrency goals, current infra, and we'll talk tradeoffs for hosted vs dedicated vs private. Then propose a benchmarking plan.
[00:27] Ravi Patel: High level, our main use case is fraud detection assistant and realtime auth messages. Typical response length is ~150-300 tokens, some streaming. We need p95 latency under 250 ms for 256-token outputs, and support 200 qps at peak with 8 concurrent streams per user.
[00:45] Maya Thompson: Okay, p95 under 250 ms for 256 tokens is fairly aggressive, especially if you're streaming the tokens, but we can unpack. Do you mean end-to-end from API call to first token or final token?
[00:55] Sara Alvarez: End-to-end first token visible to client. We stream token-by-token. If that's impossible, we can adjust to 300 ms, but 250 is the target because of UX.
[01:05] Liam Chen: Noted. Some quick context: with Redwood Hosted we manage routing, caching, and autoscaling. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools and lower jitter. Private lets you run in VPC / on-prem for data residency. Latency variance often comes from network hop and queuing.
[01:20] Omar Ruiz: For models, we're leaning to an open Llama-like 70B quantized to int8 or q4 when possible. We run shorter contexts, like 512 tokens max, seq len for generation is 256 typical. How do those runtimes look?
[01:34] Liam Chen: For a 70B model quantized, token/sec on a single high-end A100 or H100 varies: for greedy sampling you might see ~150-400 tokens/sec depending on kernel selection and sequence length. For streaming first-token to client we usually see a cold p95 higher due to KV-cache warmup. For p95 sub-250ms first-token for 256 token outputs you'll likely need model variants, smaller context model, or dedicated low-latency instance with batching disabled for those requests.
[01:55] Ravi Patel: When you say batching disabled, is that per route? We need to mix bursty interactive requests with some batch scoring jobs.
[02:03] Liam Chen: Yes route-level policies. You can configure SLOs per route. We can route interactive low-latency traffic to nodes with minimal batching and small beam size, and route scoring jobs to batch workers with higher throughput.
[02:14] Nina Gomez: From security side, we need SOC2, SSO (SAML/Okta), KMS/HSM for key management, audit logs with retention 1 year, and the ability to keep data in our VPC for PII. How does Redwood support that?
[02:28] Maya Thompson: We support SOC2 compliance documents; SSO via SAML + SCIM + RBAC; KMS integrations for private deployments and Dedicated (customer-managed KMS is supported), and audit logs in Console with export. For Hosted there are options for data retention and low-retention modes but if you need strict VPC-only storage then Private is recommended. We'll share the SOC2 summary and KMS notes after the call.
[02:48] Nina Gomez: Good. Also encryption at rest and in transit, HSM integration is a must for us.
[02:54] Liam Chen: Noted.
[02:58] Sara Alvarez: Back to latency, can you walk through a quick math: if we need p95 250ms first-token for 256-token outputs at 200 qps, what does Dedicated sizing look like?
[03:10] Liam Chen: Sure. Couple of variables: model choice, hardware (A100 vs H100), quantization, batching window, and network. For strict low-latency first-token, you want minimal batching, fast kernels, and GPUs with high single-stream perf. Ballpark: on H100 a tuned 13B/33B quantized model can reach first-token <100ms and sustained generation for 256 tokens with streaming around 200-400ms depending on sampling; a 70B quantized model is heavier — first-token could be 120-300ms. For your 200 qps with 8 concurrent streams per user, you need concurrent slots roughly equal to QPS * concurrency = 1600 concurrent streams which is high. But often concurrency per request doesn't multiply across all QPS because many requests are short-lived.
[03:50] Sara Alvarez: 1600 sounds huge. Our current estimate of concurrency was wrong maybe. Our real concurrency is closer to 5 active streams per user and expected peak qps 80. That reduces concurrent slots to 400.
[04:02] Ravi Patel: Can caching help? We have many repeated prefixes for auth prompts.
[04:07] Liam Chen: Yes. Redwood supports prefix/KV caching. If a high proportion of tokens are cached your effective token/sec improves a lot and p95 drops. We can instrument that in the benchmark.
[04:16] Omar Ruiz: For the benchmark, can we run a token/sec test with our prompt sets, sequence lengths 128 and 256, both greedy and sampling, and measure p50/p95/p99? Also include streaming and non-streaming modes.
[04:29] Maya Thompson: Absolutely. Typical benchmarking plan: customer provides sample prompt sets and traffic profile, Redwood runs a suite across Hosted test harness and a Dedicated staging pool, measuring latencies and tokens/sec, and produces a spreadsheet with p50/p95/p99 and cost estimates. We'll try to include cold starts and warmed KV-cache scenarios.
[04:45] Ravi Patel: What about batching window — how does that affect p95?
[04:48] Liam Chen: Batching increases throughput at cost of latency. If you set batching window to, say, 10 ms and allow small batches you'll get better throughput but added latency. For interactive SLOs we default batching small or disabled. The Console allows per-route batching config and intelligent suggestions via Redwood Optimize.
[05:02] Nina Gomez: For Dedicated, what are SLAs — do you offer p95 latency guarantees?
[05:06] Maya Thompson: We offer uptime SLAs and latency targets per-plan; strict p95 latency guarantees are a combination of Dedicated sizing plus routing policies. We'll provide a proposal for your target p95 and include fallbacks (smaller model variants) in case of load.
[05:18] Sara Alvarez: Pricing is important: we need Hosted cost and Dedicated reserved example for the throughput you recommend.
[05:23] Maya Thompson: We'll provide ballpark pricing for both. Generally Dedicated is more predictable cost per month; Hosted is lower friction and good for piloting. We'll include cost per 1M tokens and reserved GPU pool estimates.
[05:34] Omar Ruiz: Any pitfalls when using quantized weights with streaming? We've seen hallucination or quality regressions at q4.
[05:42] Liam Chen: Yep, quantization can change output quality slightly; we run evals on your eval set in the benchmarking plan and include regression alerts. For production we recommend running A/B between quantized and float and using Redwood Optimize suggestions.
[05:54] Ravi Patel: For networking, we want low egress latency — region matters. We are mostly US-west.
[06:00] Maya Thompson: We'll route you to our US-west dedicated pools; if Private we can colocate in your VPC region to minimize hop time.
[06:07] Sara Alvarez: Okay good. A couple transcriptions notes: sometimes product names get swapped — is Redwood Dedicated the same as "Reserved capacity"?
[06:14] Maya Thompson: Yes, Dedicated = reserved GPU pools. Private = deployed in your VPC or on-prem. Hosted = our multi-tenant API.
[06:20] Liam Chen: We'll also log per-token timing breakdowns (kernel, queuing, network) so you can see where p95 is spent.
[06:28] Nina Gomez: I want an architecture doc for Private deployment — network diagram, KMS flow, audit log retention — can you share that?
[06:34] Maya Thompson: Yes, we'll attach the Private deployment architecture and a SOC2/ISO summary.
[06:38] Sara Alvarez: Great. Can you do a quick sketch of expected numbers for our adjusted targets: p95 300ms first-token, 256 tokens, peak qps 80, concurrency 5?
[06:48] Liam Chen: Rough estimate: with a tuned 33B quantized on H100 and minimal batching, first-token p95 ~80-140ms depending on network; end-to-end finish for 256 tokens streaming p95 ~200-350ms. For 80 qps and concurrency 5 -> ~400 concurrent streams; with 33B you might need ~6-10 H100 nodes depending on token mix and caching. With 70B quantized you'd need more. We'll run exact numbers in the benchmark.
[07:12] Sara Alvarez: That sounds reasonable.
[07:15] Maya Thompson: Recap and next steps: 1) Omar/Ravi to share prompt sets and traffic profile, 2) Redwood (Liam) to run benchmarking across Hosted test harness + Dedicated staging and return spreadsheet, 3) Maya to share SOC2/KMS/Private deployment docs and pricing ballpark, 4) schedule 90-min deep technical benchmark meeting next week.
[07:35] Ravi Patel: We'll send files by end of day tomorrow.
[07:38] Nina Gomez: We'll also share security questionnaire if you want to start that.
[07:41] Maya Thompson: Perfect. Thanks everyone.
